# OctoMac

> OctoMac is a free, open source Mac app (SwiftUI, macOS 15 or newer, Apple silicon and Intel) for controlling and monitoring 3D printers that run OctoPrint. It shows several printers at once, with live temperatures, progress, cameras, a 3D G-code preview, file management, history and statistics, notifications, widgets and plugin support. It needs an OctoPrint admin account and talks to OctoPrint directly over your network; it has no servers or accounts of its own.

This file is generated by scripts/make-llms-full.sh from: README.md PRIVACY.md CONTRIBUTING.md CLAUDE.md.

</picture>

**A friendly Mac app for your OctoPrint 3D printers.**

OctoMac puts all of your [OctoPrint](https://octoprint.org) printers in one place, with a design built for watching and running prints rather than a web page squeezed into a window. Keep an eye on every printer at a glance, start a print in a couple of clicks, and watch it build up in 3D as it goes.

**[octomac-app.github.io](https://octomac-app.github.io/)**

![OctoMac showing a print in progress](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/overview.png)

## What it does

- **All your printers, side by side.** Add as many OctoPrint servers as you like. Each one shows its status, temperatures and print progress in the sidebar, switching between them is instant, and **All printers** shows every camera and print at once.
- **Live updates.** OctoMac listens to OctoPrint's live connection, so temperatures, progress and events appear the moment they happen. No waiting, no refreshing.
- **A clear overview.** See the webcam (switch between cameras if you have more than one, with a cinema mode, one-click snapshots, GIF and MP4 clips, and a picture in picture window that floats above your other apps), the current print with time left and when it'll finish, and a temperature chart you can hover over and export as PNG or SVG.
- **Print in a couple of clicks.** Browse your files as thumbnails, filter by name, open one to check its print time, filament and history, then press Print.
- **Plan prints and line them up.** Schedule a print so it's done by a time that suits you ("finish by 8am"), and queue up files for a printer. When one finishes, OctoMac asks you to clear the bed, then starts the next.
- **Notes and ratings.** Rate a print and note what worked, such as "needs a brim". It's shown next to the file the next time you print it.
- **Easy uploads and tidy folders.** Drag G-code onto the Files tab to upload it, or open a `.gcode` file from Finder (or drop it on OctoMac in the Dock) and pick a printer. Drag files onto folders to organise them. Send a file to another printer, or to several at once, and start it printing there if you like.
- **History, statistics and timelapses.** The History tab shows how many prints finished, the hours and filament they took, and a month-by-month chart for one printer or all of them. It lists what you've printed lately and whether it finished, and plays, saves or deletes OctoPrint's timelapse videos.
- **Your own buttons.** Custom controls set up in OctoPrint appear on the Move tab, including ones that ask for a value first.
- **G-code preview.** See exactly what will be printed, layer by layer or as a 3D model you can spin around.
- **Watch prints live.** While printing, the 3D preview follows along, with a little nozzle gliding along the toolpath at the printer's own pace. If you're watching the layer being printed, the view moves up with the nozzle.
- **GIFs and videos from the camera.** Record a GIF or MP4 of the last 10 seconds, the next few seconds, or a quick timelapse of a whole layer or more, then save, copy or share it.
- **Layer alerts.** Pause at a layer to drop in magnets, nuts or a new colour, or just get a notification when the print reaches it. Once the first layer is down, OctoMac sends a picture of it with Pause and Stop Print buttons, so a bad start never runs for hours.
- **Tweak a print as it runs.** Nudge the print speed and flow right from the Overview while you watch.
- **Notifications.** Get a Mac notification when a print finishes or fails, when the printer needs you (a filament change, a paused print, an MMU filament choice), if it stops answering, or if the Raspberry Pi is short of power. Finished, failed and paused prints, the first layer and your layer alerts come with a picture from the camera. Choose which ones you want in Settings.
- **Know your machine.** The Machine tab shows the printer's firmware, the Raspberry Pi's power and temperature health, the bed level map with its history (compare today's bed with an earlier measurement to see what's moved), OctoPrint and plugin updates you can install with one click, your plugins (add new ones from OctoPrint's official plugin list, switch them on or off, or uninstall them), and OctoPrint's logs, which you can read or save. If the printer won't connect, OctoMac tells you why in plain words.
- **Full control.** Heat up with your saved presets, move the print head, extrude filament, adjust fan and speed, send G-code from the console, and manage the connection and the Raspberry Pi.
- **A friendlier console.** Hide the chatter you don't need (temperatures, SD status, positions, wait and busy replies, MMU chatter) using OctoPrint's own filters, and highlight the lines you care about, including the printer's replies to your own commands. The console holds still while you scroll up to read, and a G-code cheat sheet slides out beside it with plain explanations of common commands.
- **Safe by design.** Stopping a print asks you to confirm and shows what you'd lose, and there's a separate emergency stop for when something goes wrong.
- **Widgets.** Add OctoMac to your desktop or Notification Centre to see each printer's progress, time left and temperatures, with a camera picture in the large size. On macOS 26 there's a Control Centre control too.
- **A menu bar helper.** Check on every printer from the menu bar without opening the main window.
- **Progress on the Dock icon.** A bar across OctoMac's Dock icon shows how far along the print that finishes soonest is.
- **Keyboard shortcuts.** ⌥⌘1 to ⌥⌘9 jump between printers and ⌥⌘0 shows them all. ⌥⌘P pauses or resumes the print on screen, and ⌥⌘C pops its camera out into picture in picture. ⌘1 to ⌘6 switch tabs.
- **Celsius or Fahrenheit.** Celsius by default; switch in Settings.
- **In your language.** OctoMac speaks English (UK and US), Welsh, Czech, Danish, Dutch, Finnish, French, German, Italian, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Spanish and Swedish. It follows your Mac's language, falling back to UK English, and you can choose a different one in **Settings → General**.

![The 3D G-code preview following a live print](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/live-preview.png)

![Layer alerts: pause or get a notification at a layer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/layer-alerts.png)

![All printers, side by side](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/all-printers.png)

![The History tab, with recent prints and timelapses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/history.png)

![The console with the G-code cheat sheet open](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/console.png)

![The Machine tab, with the bed level map and Raspberry Pi health](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/machine.png)

## Getting started

### What you need

- A Mac running **macOS 15 Sequoia** or newer
- One or more printers running **OctoPrint** (for example on an OctoPi Raspberry Pi)
- An **OctoPrint admin account** for OctoMac to use. OctoMac expects full access (settings, system commands, logs and so on) and isn't designed for accounts with limited permissions.

### Download

Grab the latest **OctoMac.dmg** from the [Releases page](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/releases), open it, and drag OctoMac into your Applications folder. It runs on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. OctoMac checks for new versions once a day and asks before installing one; you can turn that off in **Settings → General**.

### Or use Homebrew

```sh
brew tap octomac-app/tap
brew trust octomac-app/tap
brew install --cask octomac
```

`brew trust` lets Homebrew load the OctoMac tap; Homebrew 7 and later ask for it for any tap outside their own. OctoMac still updates itself, so there's no need for `brew upgrade`.

### Or build it yourself

You'll need **Xcode 16** or newer.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac.git
cd OctoMac
scripts/build-app.sh
open build/OctoMac.app
```

The finished app is at `build/OctoMac.app`. Drag it into your Applications folder to keep it.

You can also open `Package.swift` in Xcode and press Run.

### Add your first printer

1. Click **Add your first printer**.
2. Pick your printer from **On your network** (OctoMac finds OctoPrint servers on your local network automatically), or type its address, such as `octopi.local` or `http://192.168.1.50`. HTTPS works too: if your OctoPrint uses a self-signed certificate, OctoMac shows its fingerprint and asks whether to trust it, then only ever accepts that exact certificate from that printer.
3. Choose **Request access** and sign in to OctoPrint as an admin. Your browser opens OctoPrint, where you approve OctoMac with one click. (Prefer to paste an API key instead? Choose **Paste a key**.)
4. That's it. Your printer appears in the sidebar.

**Reaching OctoPrint from outside your home?** If it's behind a reverse proxy that asks for its own sign-in (nginx or Caddy with a password, Cloudflare Access and so on), open **Sign-in** when adding the printer and enter the user name and password, or the headers it needs, such as `CF-Access-Client-Id` and `CF-Access-Client-Secret`. OctoMac sends them only to that printer's address.

Your API keys stay on your Mac. They're kept in the macOS Keychain, protected by your login password. If you'd rather not use the Keychain, switch it off in **Settings → Printers** and OctoMac keeps them in an encrypted file only your account can read instead. See [PRIVACY.md](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/blob/master/PRIVACY.md) for exactly what OctoMac stores, and what it doesn't.

### Just looking?

Try OctoMac without a printer: choose **Help → Try Demo Mode**. Your own printers stay saved, and **Exit demo** brings them back. You can also start straight into demo mode:

```sh
open build/OctoMac.app --args --demo
```

Demo mode shows four pretend printers, including one that's busy printing and a four-hotend tool-changer, so you can explore every screen safely.

## Plugin support

OctoMac works with a standard OctoPrint install, and it gets better with a few popular plugins.

| Plugin | What OctoMac does with it | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Slicer Thumbnails](https://plugins.octoprint.org/plugins/prusaslicerthumbnails/) | Shows the picture your slicer embeds in each G-code file, in the file list, the file browser, the file info panel and while printing. Works with PrusaSlicer, SuperSlicer, OrcaSlicer, Cura and others. | Supported |
| Application Keys (built in) | Lets you connect a printer by approving OctoMac in your browser, with no copying and pasting of API keys. | Supported |
| Classic Webcam (built in) | Shows your camera stream, including your flip and rotate settings. | Supported |
| Logging (built in) | Lists OctoPrint's log files on the Machine tab, so you can read the latest lines or save a whole log. | Supported |
| Pi Support (built in) | Shows the Raspberry Pi model and warns when it's short of power or too hot. | Supported |
| Software Update (built in) | Shows whether OctoPrint and your plugins are up to date, and installs updates with one click. | Supported |
| Plugin Manager (built in) | Lists your plugins on the Machine tab, where you can add plugins from OctoPrint's official list, switch them on or off or uninstall them. | Supported |
| [Bed Level Visualizer](https://plugins.octoprint.org/plugins/bedlevelvisualizer/) | Shows your bed mesh on the Machine tab as a colour map with every probe point's height, or as a 3D surface you can turn. Measure the bed again with one click, and pick the measuring G-code from ready-made starting points. | Supported |
| [Print Time Genius](https://plugins.octoprint.org/plugins/PrintTimeGenius/) | Uses its much more accurate print times for files and time left, and says when a time comes from it. Without it, OctoMac uses OctoPrint's own estimates. | Supported |
| [Cancel Objects](https://plugins.octoprint.org/plugins/cancelobject/) | While printing several parts at once, shows them on a map of the bed and lets you stop one that's failed while the others carry on. | Supported |
| [DisplayLayerProgress](https://plugins.octoprint.org/plugins/DisplayLayerProgress/) | Shows the real layer number while printing (for example "Layer 92 of 146, about 58s each"), and makes layer alerts and the first-layer check possible. | Supported |
| [Prusa MMU](https://plugins.octoprint.org/plugins/prusammu/) | When a print starts on a printer with a Prusa Multi Material Unit, asks which filament to use, showing your filament names and colours and a countdown. You can answer from any screen, or press the slot's number. The loaded filament also shows next to the printer's name. | Supported |

Don't have a plugin installed? No problem. OctoMac simply skips that feature. For example, without Slicer Thumbnails your files show a tidy icon instead of a picture.

Want OctoMac to support a plugin you use? Open an issue and tell us about it.

### Bed Level Visualizer: measuring the bed

Bed Level Visualizer needs to know which G-code makes your printer probe the bed and report the result. In OctoMac, open the **Machine** tab and choose **G-code…** in the Bed level panel. Pick a starting point, then save:

- **Prusa MK3S and MK2.5S:** `@BEDLEVELVISUALIZER`, `G28 W`, `G80`, `G81`
- **Marlin with a probe:** `@BEDLEVELVISUALIZER`, `G28`, `G29 T`
- **Marlin with a saved mesh:** `@BEDLEVELVISUALIZER`, `M420 V`

The `@BEDLEVELVISUALIZER` line tells the plugin to start listening for the printer's report. For other printers, see the plugin's [G-code examples](https://github.com/jneilliii/OctoPrint-BedLevelVisualizer/blob/master/wiki/gcode-examples.md) and [guide](https://github.com/jneilliii/OctoPrint-BedLevelVisualizer/blob/master/wiki/index.md).

The commands are saved in OctoPrint, so the plugin's own page uses them too. Then press **Measure bed**. Measuring works while the printer is idle; the bed is most accurate when it's already at printing temperature.

### Prusa MMU: choosing a filament

If your printer has a Prusa Multi Material Unit and the [Prusa MMU](https://plugins.octoprint.org/plugins/prusammu/) plugin is installed, OctoMac asks which filament to use when a single-colour print starts.

![OctoMac asking which filament to use](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/master/docs/screenshots/mmu-filament.png)

- **It pops up wherever you are.** The question appears over the window whichever printer or tab you're looking at, and names the printer and file that are waiting.
- **Your filaments, as you set them up.** Each slot shows the name and colour you entered in the plugin's settings, and the filament that's loaded right now is marked.
- **Click or type.** Click a filament, or press its slot number on the keyboard.
- **A countdown keeps you in the loop.** You see how long is left before the plugin's timeout, and what happens if you don't choose: either the printer asks on its own screen, or the print uses the filament it was sliced with, depending on how the plugin is set up.
- **Rather use the printer?** Press **Choose on the printer** (or Escape) to close the question and pick on the printer itself. If the plugin allows it, you'll see **Use sliced filament** instead, which starts the print with the filament chosen in your slicer.
- **See what's loaded.** While printing, the loaded filament's name and colour appear next to the printer's name.

To set it up, install the Prusa MMU plugin (Machine tab → Plugins → Add plugins…, or OctoPrint's Plugin Manager) and add your filament names and colours in its settings. OctoMac picks them up automatically.

## Good to know

- **Your data stays with you.** OctoMac only talks to the OctoPrint servers you add. There are no accounts, no tracking and no cloud service. The details are in [PRIVACY.md](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/blob/master/PRIVACY.md).
- **Found a problem?** Choose **Help → Report a Problem…** and open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/issues). That's the only place we take bug reports. [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) has more on helping out.
- **Can't reach your printers?** macOS asks before an app can use your local network. If OctoMac shows that macOS is blocking it (this can happen after an update), open **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Local Network** and switch OctoMac off and on again.
- **Live preview is an estimate.** The animated nozzle follows the part of the file OctoPrint has sent to the printer. Printers keep a few moves in a small buffer, so on short moves the on-screen nozzle can run a fraction of a second ahead of the real one.
- **G-code preview downloads the file.** To show a preview, OctoMac downloads the G-code from your printer. Files are kept in memory while the app is open, so opening the same preview again is instant.

## For developers

OctoMac is written in Swift with SwiftUI, and the 3D preview uses Metal.

| Folder | What's inside |
| --- | --- |
| `Sources/OctoPrintKit` | A standalone Swift library for the OctoPrint REST API, live updates, the Application Keys sign-in flow, and a fast G-code reader |
| `Sources/OctoMac` | The Mac app: printers, screens, the 3D preview and the design system |
| `Tests/OctoPrintKitTests` | Tests for the library. Run them with `swift test` |
| `scripts/` | Build the app, and draw the app icon and logo |

Handy commands:

```sh
swift build                    # build everything
swift test                     # run the tests
scripts/build-app.sh debug     # build a debug copy of the app
```

The OctoPrint API is documented at [docs.octoprint.org](https://docs.octoprint.org/en/main/api/index.html).

<!-- PRIVACY.md -->

# Privacy

OctoMac is built to keep your data on your own Mac and your own network.

## What OctoMac talks to

- **Your OctoPrint servers, and nothing else.** OctoMac only connects to the printers you add. There are no accounts, no analytics, no tracking, no adverts and no OctoMac servers.
- **GitHub, to check for updates**, once a day unless you turn it off in Settings → General. OctoMac fetches the list of versions (`appcast.xml`) and, if you choose to update, downloads the new version from GitHub Releases. Sparkle, the updater, doesn't send any information about you or your Mac.
- **Links you choose to open**, such as a plugin's guide or GitHub, open in your web browser.

## What OctoMac stores

All of this stays on your Mac:

- **Your printers' names and addresses**, in OctoMac's preferences.
- **Your API keys**, in the macOS Keychain, protected by your login password and readable only by OctoMac. If you switch off **Settings → Printers → Keep API keys in the Keychain**, they're kept in `~/Library/Application Support/OctoMac/api-keys.dat` instead, readable only by your user account and encrypted with a key built into the app. Because OctoMac is open source, that built-in key is public, so the file stops a casual look rather than a determined attacker. A proxy sign-in (user name, password or headers) you add for a printer is stored the same way, alongside its API key, and is only ever sent to that printer's address. (If you build OctoMac yourself without a Developer ID, it uses the file by default, as macOS would otherwise ask for Keychain permission after every rebuild.)
- **A small status file for the widgets** in `~/Library/Application Support/OctoMac/Widgets/`: printer names, states, progress, temperatures and a small camera picture. Only OctoMac's own widgets read it.
- **A list of the prints OctoMac has seen finish or fail** in `~/Library/Application Support/OctoMac/History/`: file names, dates, how long they took and how much filament they used, for the statistics in the History tab. It's deleted when you remove the printer.
- **Your plans and notes for each printer** in `~/Library/Application Support/OctoMac/Printers/`: a scheduled print, the print queue, your ratings and notes on files, and earlier bed level measurements. It's deleted when you remove the printer.
- **Your choices**, such as console filters, highlights and notification settings.
- **G-code previews and thumbnails** are kept in memory while OctoMac is open, and are not saved.
- **The last few seconds of each camera** are kept in memory, so you can make a clip of something that just happened. Clips you record are made on your Mac and kept in a temporary folder until you save, copy or share them, or close the clip window; nothing is uploaded.

## Notifications

Notifications are shown by macOS on your Mac only. They aren't sent anywhere else. Finished, failed and paused prints, the first layer and your layer alerts include a picture from the printer's camera, which macOS keeps with the notification until you clear it. You can turn the pictures off in **Settings → Notifications**.

## Bug reports

**Help → Report a Problem…** writes a diagnostics file that you can read before sharing. It includes the OctoMac and macOS versions, your Mac's chip, and each printer's OctoPrint version, plugins, firmware and connection state. It leaves out printer names and addresses, API keys, proxy sign-ins, user names and file names. Nothing is sent automatically: you choose whether to attach it to a public [GitHub issue](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/issues), which is the only place we take bug reports.

<!-- CONTRIBUTING.md -->

# Contributing to OctoMac

Thanks for wanting to help! OctoMac is a small, friendly project, and bug reports, ideas and pull requests are all welcome.

## Reporting a bug

Bug reports live in [GitHub issues](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac/issues), and only there. Please don't send reports by email or anywhere else.

1. In OctoMac, choose **Help → Report a Problem…**. OctoMac writes a short diagnostics file and opens a new issue for you.
2. Describe what you did, what you expected, and what happened instead. Screenshots help a lot.
3. Attach the diagnostics file if you're happy to. Read it first: it's plain text, and OctoMac leaves out anything personal (printer addresses, API keys, user names and file names), but it's your call.

Please don't paste API keys, passwords, printer addresses or anything else private into an issue. Issues are public.

## Suggesting a feature

Open an issue and tell us what you'd like and why. If it's about an OctoPrint plugin, a link to the plugin helps.

## Building OctoMac

You'll need a Mac running macOS 15 or newer and Xcode 16 or newer.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/OctoMac-App/OctoMac.git
cd OctoMac
scripts/build-app.sh debug     # builds build/OctoMac.app
open build/OctoMac.app
swift test                     # runs the tests
```

No printer handy? Start OctoMac with `--demo`, or choose **Help → Try Demo Mode**. You get four pretend printers to try every screen on.

## Making a change

- Keep pull requests focused: one fix or feature each.
- Match the style of the code around your change. The app is SwiftUI, and the colours, fonts and shared controls live in `Sources/OctoMac/Design`.
- `Sources/OctoPrintKit` is a standalone library for the OctoPrint API. Anything that talks to OctoPrint belongs there, with a test in `Tests/OctoPrintKitTests` where it makes sense.
- Every piece of text people can see must be translatable. In SwiftUI, a string literal in `Text`, `Button`, `Label` and the like already is; text built in code uses `String(localized:)`. Data from OctoPrint or the printer (names, file names, its own messages) is shown as it is with `Text(verbatim:)`. Then run `scripts/extract-strings.sh` to add new text to `Support/Localization/Localizable.xcstrings`, and translate it into every language: `scripts/translations.py export DIR` lists what's missing, and `scripts/translations.py import DIR` merges translation files back in. GitHub Actions fails if any text isn't in the catalog or isn't translated into every language. OctoMac is translated into everything or nothing.
- Write for people, not programmers. Text in the app and the README should be plain, friendly English. Please don't use long dashes; a comma, colon or full stop reads better.
- Run `swift test` and try your change in the app (demo mode is fine) before opening the pull request.
- Every push and pull request is built and tested on GitHub Actions. One of the tests checks that **Help → Report a Problem…** never includes printer names, addresses, API keys, user names or file names, so please keep it passing.

## Releases

Releases are tagged `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (for example `v0.2.0`), and the version number lives in the `VERSION` file. Maintainers build them with `scripts/release.sh`, which makes a universal app (Apple silicon and Intel) and a disk image. Signing details are kept in a local, untracked `scripts/release.local` file and never committed; copy `scripts/release.local.example` to start one. Updates reach people through Sparkle: `scripts/release.sh --notarize --publish --notes notes.md` signs the disk image with the maintainer's update key (kept in their Keychain, never in the repository), publishes the GitHub release, adds it to `appcast.xml`, and points the Homebrew cask in [OctoMac-App/homebrew-tap](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/homebrew-tap) at the new version.

The website's source is in `website/`, and it uses the screenshots in `docs/screenshots`. `scripts/publish-site.sh` copies it to [OctoMac-App/octomac-app.github.io](https://github.com/OctoMac-App/octomac-app.github.io), which GitHub Pages serves at https://octomac-app.github.io/; run it after changing the site or its screenshots. The site is styled to look like the app, so it uses the same colours, fonts and shapes as `Sources/OctoMac/Design`. (`docs/index.html` only forwards the old address, https://octomac-app.github.io/OctoMac/, to the new one.)

## Code of conduct

Be kind and assume good intent. We're all here because we like making things.

<!-- CLAUDE.md -->

# OctoMac

A SwiftUI Mac app for OctoPrint 3D printers. This is a public repository: never commit personal details, printer addresses, API keys, signing identities, team IDs or anything from `scripts/release.local`.

## Build and test

```sh
export DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer   # swift test needs Xcode's toolchain, not just the Command Line Tools
swift build
swift test                     # Swift Testing; all tests must pass
scripts/build-app.sh debug     # assembles build/OctoMac.app (with the widget extension and Sparkle)
open build/OctoMac.app --args --demo            # demo mode: four pretend printers, no network
open build/OctoMac.app --args --demo --select 2 # start on the second demo printer
```

Use demo mode to check UI changes. It never touches the network, saved printers or stored keys.

Each new build is a new binary to macOS, which can silently block its local network access (`URLError -1009`) until the user switches OctoMac off and on in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Local Network. The app explains this when it happens. Don't change privacy settings for the user.

## Layout

- `Sources/OctoPrintKit`: a standalone client library for OctoPrint, with no app or UI code. Covers the REST API (`Endpoints/`), push updates over the websocket (`Push.swift`), Application Keys (`AppKeys.swift`), self-signed certificate pinning (`CertificateTrust.swift`), plugin APIs (`Plugins/`) and a fast G-code parser (`GCode/`). Anything that talks to OctoPrint belongs here, with tests in `Tests/OctoPrintKitTests`.
- `Sources/OctoMac/Model`: app state. `PrinterSession` holds everything live for one printer, `InstanceStore` the list of printers. API keys and proxy sign-ins live in `CredentialStore` (the Keychain by default for Developer ID builds; an encrypted file for ad-hoc builds or if the user switches the Keychain off), never in `UserDefaults`. Per-printer plans and history (the scheduled print, queue, notes and ratings, bed mesh history) live in `PrinterJournal`, one JSON file per printer; finished and failed prints for statistics live in `PrintLog`.
- `Sources/OctoMac/Views`: one file per tab or panel. `Sources/OctoMac/Design` holds the palette, fonts and shared controls; use them rather than system defaults.
- `Sources/OctoMacWidgets` and `Sources/WidgetData`: the widget extension, which reads a status file the app writes. It's linked with `NSExtensionMain` (see `Package.swift`); without that, macOS's extension loader crashes it.
- `docs/`: README images and screenshots, plus `docs/index.html`, which only forwards the old website address to the new one.
- `website/`: the website, served at https://octomac-app.github.io/ from `OctoMac-App/octomac-app.github.io`. Never edit that repository; change `website/` and run `scripts/publish-site.sh`. The site deliberately looks like the app: reuse the palette and fonts from `Sources/OctoMac/Design/Theme.swift`, and update its feature text and screenshots along with the README.
- `scripts/`: `build-app.sh` and `assemble.sh` package the app; `release.sh` makes notarised releases, updates `appcast.xml` and the Homebrew cask in `OctoMac-App/homebrew-tap` (maintainers only; signing settings come from the untracked `scripts/release.local`, see `release.local.example`).

## Conventions

- Match the surrounding code: its naming, comment density and SwiftUI style.
- Everything people can see in the app is translated into all 15 languages (UK English is the source; see `scripts/translations.py`). New text must be marked for translation (a literal in a SwiftUI view, or `String(localized:)`), extracted with `scripts/extract-strings.sh`, and translated before it ships; CI fails otherwise. Data from OctoPrint, printers or files uses `Text(verbatim:)`. Numbers, durations and dates use the formatters in `Fmt` or Foundation's, never `String(format:)`, so they follow the language.
- Text in the app, README and comments is plain, friendly British English, written for people rather than programmers. Never use long (em) dashes; use a comma, colon or full stop. CI fails if one appears.
- Bug reports are GitHub issues only. Help → Report a Problem builds a diagnostics file that must never include printer names, addresses, API keys, proxy sign-ins, user names or file names; `DiagnosticsPrivacyTests` enforces this.
- OctoPrint plugins are optional: check a plugin is present before using it, and fall back gracefully when it isn't.
- Out of scope unless the maintainer asks: power control and smart plugs, Spoolman, and accounts with limited OctoPrint permissions (OctoMac expects an admin account).
- Keep pull requests focused, and update the README, `PRIVACY.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md` when a change affects them. After editing any of those or this file, run `scripts/make-llms-full.sh` to rebuild `llms-full.txt` (CI checks it's current).
